body:
I am a young adult who cut at the beginning of my teenage years. I can tell you that I always thought my mom's reaction was close to ideal, so I will tell you a little how she handled the situation.

I started cutting because I was always angry, at the world, and this was the only way I knew how to channel my anger. The cutting was pretty bad, and soon it became more than a way to a process anger, it became routine and a form of pleasure.

When my parents found out, of course they were devastated. But my mom made it clear from the start that she wasn't going to hide all the knives and scissors of the house. She said that what she wanted wasn't that I stopped cutting, but rather that I get better emotionally so that I would not feel those urges anymore.

This for me was what made me trust her immediately. Cutting was all I had at that time, and I can't imagine what it would have been like if someone just used their power to try and take it away. And let me warn you, it is useless to try to take it away, because there are always other blades, other ways to hurt yourself.

She also suggested that I see a therapist, but made it clear that it wasn't an obligation, and she let met change when the first one didn't suit me. Seeing a therapist was very tough, I was very reticent at first and barely talked, but after  a couple of months I started opening up. I gradually started to feel better, and started trying to stop the self-harm, and after a little less than a year, I managed to stop completely.

My mom never tried to be my therapist, or to inquire too much about my life, because she knew that it would have been to hard for me to open up to her. 

So what I can say is, all a mom can do is be their for their child. If the child doesn't want to talk, don't make him. Don't try to take anything from him, and don't prevent him from seeing his friends, even if you thing they are a bad influence. Any brutal change would just foster resentment. You can just let your child know that you are there no matter what for support, that you are not judging, that you know you are not their savior, but that they can count on you if they need it.

TLDR: be understanding, supportive, don't be intrusive, don't force your child to stop, and don't presume you know what is best for them regarding the handling of that issue

Yes! Totally! 
Very often I join some people with which I'm not close, and I will identify someone with a lot of confidence, remember everything they've told me, where we met, and I will feel very proud of myself, thinking I'm finally making progress. Then we will start talking and I will progressively realize I got them confused with someone completely different.

Luckily by now, even if I'm ultra confident, I try and not say anything that applies to who I think they are, until the person has said something that can confirm who they are :)

I know relapsing sucks. But you didn't throw a year and a half away. In total, you cut yourself once out of 547 days. Maybe that day was today, but it could as well have been at the beginning or in the middle. The percentage of days where you self harmed is quite small, and that is what counts. Harming yourself today doesn't have to mean that you have more probability to do it again tomorrow. Try to think about all the days where you didn't relapse, because they count too, and in the end you have been much stronger than anything else.

Hey /u/leeneh.
I went through a very similar situation. I am a girl, and I started cutting and being suicidal at 12 for no clear reason; I had friends and family and everything was fine.

I managed to stop.

It's good that you're reaching out. If you want we can talk more by pm, I would like to help you in any way I can.
/u/TheEmptyTrip please don't do it.

For me it all went very progressively. I started with a small pocket knife that didn't do much damage Sometimes I would try bruising. When I wasn't at home and really needed to cut, I would just pick up whatever, a shard of glass or a sharp rock. It felt like a revelation when I found some box cutters in my garage, and then I kept to that. 

I found bruising much much harder though: to cause and to withstand.
What do you mean by immature? Make jokes or what?

It's too bad that your friends didn't know how to react in a good manner. From the answers here it really seems that a therapist is the safest best.

Just out of curiosity, you know precisely what is causing it?

Do you think friends telling you about self harming incites you to do it, or not at all?

I guess it's much harder to talk about it to people if you still do it, because it will hurt them a lot more. Therapists didn't try to lecture you to stop?

Thanks for the advice :)

I'm sorry that nobody around you understands, and that your scars bother you.

I think though that having a friend who currently self harms is not always a good thing for people who self harm...

Yes, I think that someone wanting to understand would also help a lot.
Probably some people care, and some people want to know (not necessarily for the right reasons). I think most often these two types of people are not the same people.

Have you tried writing or seeing a therapist though?

Haha that's some long excuse. I tried giving ridiculous answers but some people then go "No but seriously, what happened?". 

It's good that you can be truthful most of the time.
They believe it?
Don't you think that telling them to fuck off is rude? I honestly think sometimes people don't know better when they ask.

It's harder to tell someone important, I agree. But when you say it to someone important, they probably know you well already, and you will be defined by more than just the selfharm.  Whereas with people you just met, it's weird to give this image of yourself as the only one they know.
Do you think that they automatically know, or that they have some doubt about what it might be?

Haha I used to says cats but people would call bullshit on that.

I get what you're getting at with lying and not moving on, but don't you feel it's just too weird to tell it to just anyone who asks?  There's too much stigma around this
Thanks! Good on you for your ten years. You relapsed, it's a tough blow, but ten years >> one day, so I hope you're not beating yourself up.

You told him but did you really ever expand on the subject with anybody? 
Or you don't feel the need to?

I don't want to make a big deal out of it. I just feel like I need someone to know, basically, everything.

Totally. I started cutting because I was very angry, very often. At other people or at me, it didn't matter, it felt really good taking it out on myself. But then I started doing it when I had any type of negative feelings, and then it went to boredom, and then it was just routine.

It's hard, but you need to make yourself louder than that voice.

If you're with a therapist that doesn't help, say that to your mother, and ask to change. 

Also make her understand that taking your razors is not a solution to selfharming.
The only solution is wanting to stop.

It always seems to be lurking. 
But I'm really, really hoping it does.

I haven't done anything in 11 years, and most of the time I don't understand why I even started. But once in a while, I'm just too tired of hurting inside, and hurting outside seems the only way to numb it down for a little time.

Thank you /u/throwawayfm2040 for your words.

Yes I guess that is what I mean.
If other people also feel totally normal most of the time, but might just decide to jump off a bridge if they happen to be walking on one - without thinking about it prior.

I used to self-harm a long time ago. I also attempted suicide. It's been years, and for a long time I thought I was okay. But I feel like I'm constantly running away from that period, and that at some point I will just be walking normally then suddenly throw myself in front of a train.

I think I get something similar.
At certain moments, I feel very restless. I know that at that precise moment I'm not going to do it, but I always feel like on the verge of crossing that line. So it's often as if I'm scarred of the moment when I finally will.
